definition: In linguistic morphology and information retrieval, stemming is the process of reducing inflected (or sometimes derived) words to their word stem, base or root form—generally a written word form.
details: The stem need not be identical to the morphological root of the word; it is usually sufficient that related words map to the same stem, even if this stem is not in itself a valid root. Algorithms for stemming have been studied in computer science since the 1960s. Many search engines treat words with the same stem as synonyms as a kind of query expansion, a process called conflation. A computer program or subroutine that stems word may be called a stemming program, stemming algorithm, or stemmer.

explainer.lead: Stemming reduces inflected or derived words to their word stem, base or root form. It matters in search because related words can then be treated as matching.

tiers.eli5: It trims word endings so that 'running', 'runs' and 'runner' all collapse to the same core.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply stemmers so that words sharing a stem are treated as synonyms, a form of query expansion called conflation. A pitfall is that the stem need not be a valid root, so over-stemming can merge unrelated words.
tiers.paperLevel: The process of reducing inflected or sometimes derived words to their word stem, base or root form, generally a written word form; the stem need not equal the morphological root. Algorithms have been studied since the 1960s, and a program that stems words may be called a stemmer.

explainer.example: A search engine indexes 'running' under the stem 'run' and treats a query for 'runs' as a match.
